definition: Autonomous things, abbreviated AuT, or the Internet of autonomous things, abbreviated as IoAT, is an emerging term for the technological developments that are expected to bring computers into the physical environment as autonomous entities without human direction, freely moving and interacting with humans and other objects.
details: Self-navigating drones are the first AuT technology in (limited) deployment. It is expected that the first mass-deployment of AuT technologies will be the autonomous car, generally expected to be available around 2020. Other currently expected AuT technologies include home robotics (e.g., machines that provide care for the elderly, infirm or young), and military robots (air, land or sea autonomous machines with information-collection or target-attack capabilities). AuT technologies share many common traits, which justify the common notation. They are all based on recent breakthroughs in the domains of (deep) machine learning and artificial intelligence. They all require extensive and prompt regulatory developments to specify the requirements from them and to license and manage their deployment (see the further reading below). And they all require unprecedented levels of safety (e.g., automobile safety) and security, to overcome concerns about the potential negative impact of the new technology. explainer.lead: Autonomous things are computers that act in the physical world without human direction, moving and interacting with people and objects. They matter because technologies such as self-navigating drones, autonomous cars, and care robots need exceptionally strong safety, security, and regulation before widespread deployment.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a robot helper that can go about its work without someone steering it or telling it every move to make. Autonomous things are machines like that: they operate around people and objects on their own. A drone that navigates by itself is one early example.
tiers.practitioner: AuT applies recent AI and deep machine-learning advances to systems that act in physical settings without human direction. Development and deployment must address licensing, regulation, safety, and security, including both hazards removed by autonomy and new hazards it introduces.
tiers.paperLevel: AuT denotes computers embedded in the physical environment as autonomous entities that operate without human direction and can move and interact with humans and other objects. The shared challenges across AuT technologies are stringent safety and security requirements and the need for prompt regulation, licensing, and deployment management.

explainer.example: An autonomous car would travel without a person directing its every action. It could improve safety by removing major existing causes of vehicle danger, while also creating new safety and security issues that must be managed.

explainer.intuition: Instead of remaining behind a screen or following continuous human commands, a computer becomes an independent actor in the physical environment. The common idea links machines that otherwise serve very different purposes.
howItWorks: Recent AI and deep machine-learning advances provide the basis for autonomous behavior.
The machine operates in the physical environment without human direction.
It moves freely and interacts with people and other objects.
Before deployment, its safety, security, licensing, and regulatory requirements must be addressed.
explainer.whyItMatters: AuT brings AI decisions into direct physical contact with people, so failures can have physical consequences. Widespread use therefore depends not only on technical advances but also on unusually strong safety, security, and regulatory arrangements.
misconceptions: AuT is not simply another name for any internet-connected device.
It does not describe machines that depend on continuous human direction.
It concerns physical autonomous entities, not software acting only in a virtual environment.
